# Was the NSA network outage a hack?

**Debunked.** No public evidence says it was. The Director of National Intelligence says it was not a cyberattack and blames patching for PHP flaws. The NSA has given no technical detail.

Incident: NSA internal network disruption, Nov 17, 2026. Also reported as the NSA outage and the NSANet outage. First published Nov 19, 2026; last updated Nov 19, 2026, 5:20 PM ET.

> **Not verified: initial investigation only.** Nothing on this page is absolutely confirmed. It is an early look based only on publicly available sources, and it should not be treated as verified fact. Even items labeled "Confirmed" only mean a public source reports them. Made for entertainment using AI. Not endorsed by the NSA, any government agency, news outlet, company, or anyone else named.

This is the current answer, not a final verdict.

## The latest

Nov 19, 2026, 5:20 PM ET: **Officials blame patching for PHP flaws and say it was not a cyberattack; the network was reported still partly down on Nov 19.** First version of this page. Sources: NSA statement (Nov 17), White House release (Nov 18), CISA alert (Oct 21), and The Record, CBS News, NBC News, MS NOW, ABC News and PBS. nsa.gov pages not re-read: access blocked to automated fetch. Staleness check done: first run, nothing to refresh. Privacy check done: no reporter names, handles or private people.

## At a glance

- Status: monitoring
- Size: Nation-level potential. Potential only: it would be nation-level if the worst case were true, since this is the NSA's classified network. The known impact is an internal outage that kept many staff home; officials say core missions kept running and see no sign of an attack.
- Who is affected: NSA employees, mainly at Fort Meade, Maryland, and a site in Georgia, who could not use the internal network normally and were told to stagger arrivals or stay home. The public is not directly affected and there is nothing the public needs to do.

| Value | What | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 17 | NSA statement on the disruption | Routine maintenance, per the NSA |
| Oct 21 | US warning to patch PHP flaws | CISA, FBI and NSA |

### Known so far

- The NSA says it had a temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance, and that mission-critical capabilities stayed fully operational.
- The Director of National Intelligence said patching for recently found PHP flaws caused some NSA systems not to come back up as expected. This confirms what he said, not the technical detail.
- The Director of National Intelligence says the recent outages were not a cyberattack and not a coordinated nation-state effort.
- He told a House committee there is no indication of outside or state-sponsored actors behind the NSA disruption.
- In October, CISA, the FBI and the NSA urged everyone to patch two critical PHP flaws right away.

### Not known yet

- Whether the network is fully back. Reports on Nov 18 and Nov 19 differ, and the NSA has not said.
- Which systems failed, or what went wrong technically. The NSA has not said.
- How many staff were affected and for how long.
- Whether the network first failed on Monday, Nov 16, or Tuesday, Nov 17.
- Whether the NSA or the intelligence community will publish a fuller explanation.

## Official statements

> The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.
>
> — NSA statement on network issues, Nov 17

> This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state.
>
> — Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, quoted in a White House release, Nov 18

> These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
>
> — Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Nov 18, as reported by CBS News and ABC News
